terms.meaning: one triple (depth, first line, last line) for one statement
one piece of the parsed python code, such as a statement, a test, or a name
one run of code lines of the block, the unit a beat counts in
one step of the explanation, a run of cells with its own text
the chain of enclosing block names, joined with dots, that a nested name sits under
one node of the condensed call graph: a block, or a set of blocks that call each other in a cycle
one entry of the map tree, with an id like F02 and the line ranges it covers
a node for a whole block, which carries a name; the nodes under it are beats and have no name
the lines between the first and last line of a node that no child statement covers
the block made of the lines that are outside every function and class
the record of which block calls which, taken from the calls table
one top-level node of the map: the whole story of one function or of the script
a node of the map tree that has no children
one function of the file, or all the top-level code of the file together

map.name: script
map.takes: the file run from the command line
map.gives: the imported tools, the prompt text, the call counter, and the run of main()
map.story:
script imports the tools, sets PROMPT and CALLS, then calls main() when you run the file.
Example: python decompile.py decompile.py explains every block of decompile.py and writes map.json beside it.
PROMPT is the instruction text sent to Claude for one block. CALLS counts those calls. An import of this file starts nothing.
map.text: script — imports the tools, holds PROMPT and CALLS, and runs main() when the file is started as a program

children.text:
The tools this file needs:
ast — read Python source as a tree of statements
json — read the answer of the model and write map.json
re — text patterns
subprocess — start the claude command
sys — the command line and the exit
Path — the file to read and the file to write

jedi — find where each name is set and where it is used, for the links

PROMPT = the full instruction text sent to Claude for one block
It gives the file, the cells of the block and the statement ranges, then it asks for a root line, a story, terms, and beats, and it shows the JSON shape of the answer.

CALLS = a one-item list that counts the calls to Claude
The count is in a list so that ask_claude can raise it from inside, and the last report can print it.

When the file runs as a program, start main(), which reads the file named on the command line and writes map.json next to it.
When another file imports this file, nothing runs.

map.name: statements
map.takes: the file path and its source text
map.gives: one row per statement: depth, first line, last line
map.story:
statements(path, src) lists every statement of a Python file with its nesting depth and line range.
Example: for a file whose only code is a def on line 1 with one line inside it, the result is [(0, 1, 2), (1, 2, 2)].
Depth 0 means a top-level statement, and a deeper number means a statement inside another one. Rows come in source order, parent before child. For a file that is not .py the result is an empty list.
map.text: statements(path, src) -> list of (depth, start, end) — lists every Python statement in the file with its nesting depth and line range

children.text:
statements(path, src) reads the file path and its source text.
When the file is not a .py file there is no Python syntax to read, so the block gives back an empty list and stops.

rows = the list that collects one entry per statement.
Each entry will hold the depth of the statement and its first and last line.
Parse the source into a syntax tree, then let walk() fill rows with every statement under the tree, counted from depth 0.
Give rows back to the caller, in source order with each parent before its children.

map.name: statements.walk
map.takes: an AST node and the depth of its children
map.gives: nothing; it appends rows to the list of the caller
map.story:
walk(node, depth) adds one row for every statement below node, with the nesting depth of that statement.
A row is the triple (depth, first line, last line).
Example: for a def at depth 0 that holds one assignment, walk adds (1, 2, 2) for the assignment.
Statements inside a statement get depth plus one. Parts that are not statements, like an if test, do not add a row, but walk still looks inside them.
map.text: walk(node, depth) -> None — records every statement under a node with its nesting depth into rows

children.text:
walk(node, depth) looks at each direct child of node in the tree.
depth = how deep the current children are in the statement nesting.

When the child is a statement, add its row to rows: the depth, its first line and its last line.
Then walk goes into that statement with depth + 1, because the statements inside it are one level deeper.

When the child is not a statement, like an expression or a test, walk goes into it at the same depth.
This finds statements that hide below an expression without a false increase of the depth.

map.name: cells_of
map.takes: a file path, its source text, and its lines
map.gives: the cells of the file, each one a line range
map.story:
cells_of(path, src, lines) splits a file into cells: line ranges that each hold one statement.
Example: a file of `x = 1`, `if x:`, `print(x)` gives the ranges [1,1], [2,2] and [3,3].
Every non-blank line lands in exactly one cell. A comment line joins the cell below it. A file that is not Python is split at its blank lines.
map.text: cells_of(path, src, lines) -> list of cells — splits one file into the smallest line ranges a text can explain, with every non-blank line in exactly one range

children.text:
cells_of reads the file three ways: its path, its source text src, and its lines.

spans = the line ranges found so far, empty at the start.

The suffix of path picks the method: a .py file is split by its parsed statements, any other file by its blank lines.
Parse the source and hand each top-level statement to emit, which adds one line range for every leaf statement under it, plus the lines that statement keeps for itself.

When spans is still empty — the file is not Python — fall back to the blank lines.
Each run of non-blank lines becomes one span, and cells_of returns those runs as the cells.

covered = every line number the spans already hold.

extra = the runs of non-blank lines that no span holds.
These are the comments and the decorator lines the parser does not report as statements, and no line may stay outside a cell.

Each extra run joins the span below it, so a comment goes with the code it introduces.
A run with no span below it extends the end of the last span instead.
Give back the spans in line order, each one wrapped as a cell.

map.name: cells_of.kids_of
map.takes: one parsed code node
map.gives: the statement nodes under it, in file order
map.story:
kids_of(node) collects the statements directly under one AST node.
Example: for an if statement, kids_of gives the statements of its body and of its else part.
When a child is not a statement, kids_of goes into that child and takes the statements found there.
A node with no statements under it gives an empty list.
map.text: kids_of(node) -> list of statement nodes — collects the statements directly under one node, looking through the parts that are not statements

children.text:
out = the statement nodes found under node
It starts empty and fills up as the search reads the children.
read every direct child of node, one at a time

A child that is already a statement goes into out as it is.

A child that is not a statement — a test, a name, an operator — can still hold statements inside it. For such a child kids_of calls itself and adds everything that comes back, so no statement stays hidden.
return out, the statements of this node

map.name: cells_of.emit
map.takes: one parsed code node
map.gives: nothing; it adds line ranges to the spans list
map.story:
emit(node) puts the line ranges of the statements under node into the spans list.
Example: for a def on line 1 with body statements on lines 2 and 3, emit adds [2,2], [3,3], then [1,1].
A statement with no statement inside it gives one span that holds all its lines.
The own lines of a node, like the def header, become spans after the spans of its children.
Blank lines never start a span.
map.text: emit(node) -> None — appends to spans one line range for every leaf statement under node, plus the lines node keeps for itself

children.text:
kids = the statement nodes directly inside node, from kids_of(node)

emit needs them to know which lines belong to a child and which lines node holds alone.
When node has no statements inside it, node is the smallest unit: its whole line range goes to spans and the work stops here.

covered = every line number that a child statement holds

In the same loop emit calls itself on each child, so each child adds its own spans first.

Go through the lines of node from the first to the last and mark a line own when no child covers it and the line is not blank.

a = the first line of the run of own lines that is open now, or None when no run is open.
When a run of own lines ends, its range goes to spans.

When the last line of node ends with a run still open, that run goes to spans up to node.end_lineno.
Without this step the final own lines of the node would get no span.

map.name: merge
map.takes: a list of [start, end] line ranges
map.gives: the same coverage as fewer, non-touching ranges
map.story:
merge(spans) joins line ranges that overlap or sit next to each other.
Example: merge([[5, 6], [1, 3], [4, 4]]) gives [[1, 6]].
The result is sorted by start line. Two ranges join when the second starts at most one line after the first ends. Ranges with a gap of two or more lines stay apart.
map.text: merge(spans) -> list of line ranges — joins the ranges that touch or overlap into one range each

children.text:
merge(spans) takes a list of [start, end] line ranges and reads them in order of start line.

out = the ranges kept so far, each already as wide as it can be.
Sorting first means every new range can only extend the last one.

When the new range starts at most one line after the last kept range ends, the two are one run: push the end of the last range out to cover the new one.
The +1 makes ranges that only touch, like 3-4 and 5-6, join as well.
When there is a real gap, keep the new range as a separate entry.
Give back the joined ranges, sorted and with no overlaps.

map.name: ask_claude
map.takes: a prompt string
map.gives: the parsed JSON object from the answer
map.story:
ask_claude(prompt) sends one prompt to the claude command line tool and reads back a JSON object.
Example: when claude answers 'Sure: {"ok": true}', ask_claude gives the dict {"ok": True}.
The counter CALLS grows by one on every call. Text before the first brace and after the last brace is ignored. A non-zero exit code or a 600 second timeout stops the program.
map.text: ask_claude(prompt) -> dict — sends one prompt to the claude command line tool and returns the JSON object it answered with

children.text:
CALLS[0] = the running total of claude calls this run has made
Every call adds one, so the final report can print how many calls the compile cost.

r = the finished claude command, run with the prompt and --output-format json
The timeout of 600 seconds bounds one call.

The assert stops the program when claude fails, and shows the last 500 characters of its error output.

raw = the answer text claude put in the result field of its JSON envelope
The return takes the text from the first { to the last } and parses it, so any words claude wrote around the object do no harm.

map.name: check_block
map.takes: one model answer, the block cells, the statement spans, the essential lines, and the block label
map.gives: the checked root, story, terms and beats
map.story:
check_block(m, cells, stmts, ess, label) tests one model answer and returns its four parts.
Example: with 3 cells, the beat pairs [1, 2] and [3, 3] pass, but [1, 2] and [2, 3] fail.
Each failed assert carries a message that tells the model what to repair.
Every term must appear word for word in the story.
A beat may not hold only some lines of a statement.
map.text: check_block(m, cells, stmts, ess, label) -> (root, story, terms, beats) — asserts that one model answer keeps every shape rule, then hands its four parts back

children.text:
check_block(m, cells, stmts, ess, label) reads the answer m and tests it rule by rule; the first broken rule raises an error whose message tells the caller what to repair.

root = the answer's root object, the one line that stands for the whole block.
It must be a dict, because nothing else can be read out of it.

the root must hold three non-empty strings:
text — the signature line of the block
takes — the input, in a short noun phrase
gives — the output, in a short noun phrase

when label names a function, so it ends with "()", the root text must start with that name and an open bracket, so the root really reads as a signature.
The top-level script block has no signature, so this test is skipped for it.

story = the prose the reader sees.
It must be a non-empty string.

terms = the list of words the story defines.
An empty list is legal. Each entry must be a dict with a non-empty term and a non-empty meaning, and the term must appear verbatim in the story, so no definition stays unused.

beats = the list of explanation steps, which must be a list and must not be empty.

at = 1, the cell number at which the next beat must start.

each beat is tested in turn, and at moves to the cell after it, so the beats make one chain with no gap and no overlap:
its cells [a, b] must start exactly at at
b must not go past the last cell
its text must be a non-empty string

Then the beat's real line numbers are collected from its cells and cut down to ess, the essential lines. Against every statement span the beat must hold all of the statement, only lines inside it, or none of them. When it cuts a statement, the message names the cells that lie inside that statement, so the model knows where to put the border.
the last beat must end at the last cell, so together the beats cover the whole block; then the root, story, terms and beats go back to the caller as trusted parts.

map.name: carve
map.takes: a line range, the ranges to remove from it, and the file lines
map.gives: the leftover line ranges, in order, with no blank edges
map.story:
carve(a, b, minus, lines) returns the parts of the line range a..b that the minus ranges do not cover.
Example: carve(1, 10, [[3, 5]], lines) gives [[1, 2], [6, 10]].
Blank lines at the start and the end of each part are removed. A part that holds only blank lines is dropped. When minus covers everything, the result is an empty list.
map.text: carve(a, b, minus, lines) -> list of line ranges — returns the parts of the range a..b that no minus range covers, with blank edges removed

children.text:
the input is a line range a..b, the ranges in minus to take out of it, and lines, the text of the file.

The state this needs:
used = every line number that some minus range covers
spans = the free runs found so far
run = the line where the open free run started, or None when no run is open

step over line a to line b and mark a line free when used does not hold it.
A run opens at the first free line and closes at the first line that is not free, and the closed run [run, i - 1] goes into spans.
The loop goes one step past b so that a run which reaches the end still closes.

clean each free run: move its start forward while that line is blank, move its end back while that line is blank, and keep it only when a line is left.
Blank edges tell a reader nothing, and a run of only blank lines is worth nothing at all.
out = the cleaned free ranges, given back in order

map.name: blocks_of
map.takes: a file path, its source text, and its lines
map.gives: the blocks of the file, in file order
map.story:
blocks_of(path, src, lines) splits a file into one block per function or class, plus a script block.
Example: a file with def a() on lines 1-3 and a print on line 5 gives block a with lines 1-3 and block script with line 5.
A block that holds a nested function loses those lines, because the nested function is its own block. A file with no top-level code gets no script block. A file that is not python gives one script block for all of it.
map.text: blocks_of(path, src, lines) -> list of blocks — splits the file into one block for every function or class, plus a script block for the code outside them

children.text:
fns = every function and class in the file, each with its dotted name and its line span.

grab() fills fns from the parsed python source. A file that is not python leaves fns empty, so the whole file stays one block.

Make one block for each entry in fns.
inner = the line spans of the functions and classes nested inside this one.

carve() takes the function span and removes the inner spans from it, so each block keeps only its own lines and the nested ones become blocks of their own.

carve() runs once more over the whole file with every function span removed.
What is left is the top-level code, and it becomes the block named script. When nothing is left, no script block is added.
Sort the blocks by their first line and return them, so the caller reads them in file order.

map.name: blocks_of.grab
map.takes: a syntax tree node and the def names around it
map.gives: nothing; it appends records to fns
map.story:
grab(node, scope) finds every function and class under node and appends one record to fns for each.
Example: for a def blocks_of that holds a def grab, the names recorded are blocks_of, then blocks_of.grab.
The span starts at the first decorator line. Other nodes are searched with the same scope.
map.text: grab(node, scope) -> None — adds every function and class under node to fns, each with its dotted name and line span

children.text:
grab(node, scope) = the recursive search over one syntax tree node.
scope holds the names of the defs that enclose this node, so a nested def gets a dotted name.
look at each direct child of the node, one at a time

when the child is a function, an async function, or a class, record it in fns:

name — the enclosing names in scope joined with dots, plus the child's own name
span — from the first decorator line, or the def line when there is no decorator, to the last line of the body
node — the syntax tree node itself, kept for later work

Then grab calls itself on that child with the child's name added to scope, so defs inside it get dotted names.
for any other child, grab calls itself with the same scope, because a def can sit inside an if, a try, or a loop and must still be found

map.name: calls_of
map.takes: one block, the module body, and every block name
map.gives: the names this block calls, sorted
map.story:
calls_of(block, body, names) lists the blocks that one block calls.
Example: the block main uses cells_of and merge, so calls_of gives ["cells_of", "merge"].
A block never lists itself. Code inside a nested def or class belongs to that nested block. For the script block, calls_of reads only the top-level code.
map.text: calls_of(block, body, names) -> list of block names — lists the other blocks whose names this block uses

children.text:
calls_of(block, body, names) sets up three names before it reads any code:

skip = the node types that start a block of their own — function defs, async function defs, class defs
scope = the parts of the block's dotted name, like ["blocks_of", "grab"], and an empty list for the script block
out = the set that collects each block name found

run scan() on the right starting points.
A function block starts at its own node; the script block starts at each top-level statement that is not a def or a class, because those lines belong to other blocks.
Each scan(t) call adds to out every block name that the code under t uses.
give the collected names back in sorted order, so the same block always reports its calls in the same order

map.name: calls_of.resolve
map.takes: a bare name used in the code
map.gives: the matching block name, or None
map.story:
resolve(word) turns a bare name into the full name of the block that defines it.
Example: with scope ["cells_of"], resolve("emit") gives "cells_of.emit".
It tries the longest scope path first, then drops one level each time. The bare word alone is the last try. When no candidate is in names, the result is None.
map.text: resolve(word) -> block name or None — turns a bare name into the full block name that the current scope can see

children.text:
resolve(word) is the small helper that calls_of uses to give a bare name its full block name.
It reads scope, the chain of enclosing blocks, and names, the set of known block names.

Try each depth of scope, from the innermost out:
k = how many parts of scope to keep, counted down from all of them to none
hit = those parts and word joined with dots, one candidate block name

The first candidate that is in names is the answer, so a name defined inside a block wins over a top-level name that is spelled the same.
When no depth gives a known name, give back None, which tells calls_of the word points to nothing in this file.

map.name: calls_of.scan
map.takes: an AST node
map.gives: nothing; it fills the out set
map.story:
scan(node) adds to out every block name that the code under node uses.
Example: node holds x = merge(spans), and merge is a block, so out gets "merge".
scan calls itself on each child, so it finds names at any depth. It does not enter nested def or class nodes. It never adds the block's own name.
map.text: scan(node) -> None — adds to out every block name that the code under node uses

children.text: scan(node) looks at each direct child node of the AST node it gets.

A child that is a def or a class is one of the skip kinds, so scan passes over it.
Those lines belong to their own block, not to this one.

A child that is a bare name goes to resolve(), which gives the full block name that this scope can see.

hit = the block name behind the bare name, or None.

When there is a name, and it is not the block's own name, it goes into out. The block does not count as a caller of itself.
scan calls itself on the child, so names deeper in the tree also reach out.

map.name: layers_of
map.takes: the blocks and the names each block calls
map.gives: a layer number for every block name
map.story:
layers_of(blocks, calls) gives each block a layer number from the call graph.
Example: main calls carve, and carve calls nothing. Then carve is layer 1 and main is layer 2.
Blocks in a call cycle share one group, so they get the same layer. A block that calls nothing is layer 1.
map.text: layers_of(blocks, calls) -> dict of block name to int — gives every block a layer number, one more than the deepest block it calls, and puts the blocks of a call cycle on the same layer

children.text:
Set up the tables the search fills:
idx = the order number a block gets when the search first reaches it
low = the lowest order number the search can reach back to from that block
on = the names now on the stack
st = the stack of blocks the search has not yet settled
comp = the group key of each block, one key for every block of a cycle

k = the next order number, held in a one-item list so the inner search can change it

Call strong() once for every block not yet seen, so comp ends with a group key for each block.
Blocks that call each other in a cycle get the same key, so a cycle counts as one thing.

edges = the calls between groups, from one group key to the set of group keys it calls

A call that stays inside one group is dropped, so this smaller graph has no cycles and its depth is safe to measure.

h = the store of group depths already worked out, so height() computes each group once.

Ask height() for the depth of each block's group and return the block name to layer number map.

map.name: layers_of.strong
map.takes: one block name
map.gives: no value, only the filled idx, low and comp tables
map.story:
strong(v) finds the group of blocks that call each other in a cycle, starting from block v.
Example: a calls b, and b calls a. strong("a") sets comp["a"] and comp["b"] to "a".
A block in no cycle becomes a group of one. strong calls itself for each callee it has not seen. The result stays in comp.
map.text: strong(v) -> None — runs the Tarjan search from block v and gives every block of v's cycle the same key in comp

children.text:
strong(v) = one visit of the block named v in the Tarjan search.
It lives inside layers_of, so it reads and fills that block's idx, low, st, on and comp.

Number the visit and put v on the open stack:

idx[v] = the order in which v was reached
low[v] = the smallest visit number v can reach, at the start its own
k[0] = the counter for the next visit number
st = the stack of blocks whose group is not decided yet
on = the set of names now on that stack

Look at every block that v calls.
A callee that was never reached gets its own strong() visit, and v then keeps the smallest number that visit found.
A callee still on the stack shows a cycle, so v lowers its low to that callee's visit number.

When low[v] is equal to idx[v], v is the first block of its cycle group.
Pop the stack down to v and set comp[w] = v for each popped name, so all blocks of one cycle get the name v as their group key.

map.name: layers_of.height
map.takes: the key of one group in the call graph
map.gives: the number of call layers at and below that group
map.story:
height(c) gives the layer number of the group c.
Example: c calls nothing, so height(c) is 1.
When c calls only d, and height(d) is 1, height(c) is 2.
h stores each answer, so a group is counted one time only.
map.text: height(c) -> int — gives the layer number of the group c: one more than the tallest group it calls

children.text:
height(c) = the layer number of the group c.
It reads the shared tables h and edges from the block around it.

When h holds no answer for c yet, compute one: ask height for every group that c calls, keep the largest, and add one.

height calls itself here, so the count reaches all the way down the call chain.
A group that calls nothing gets 1, because max uses the default 0.
give the caller the height in h, the new one or the one that was there before

map.name: nodes_of
map.takes: the list of root nodes of a map tree
map.gives: every node of that tree in one flat list
map.story:
nodes_of(tree) puts every node of a map tree into one flat list.
Example: for one root R with children A and B, nodes_of gives [R, A, B].
A parent comes before its children. Children of children are included too. When tree is empty, the result is an empty list.
map.text: nodes_of(tree) -> list of nodes — flattens the whole map tree into one list that holds every root and every child

children.text:
out = the flat list of nodes that this block builds

It starts empty, and the helper walk fills it.
call walk on the top nodes of the tree, which adds every node and every node under it to out, then return out as the flat list.

map.name: nodes_of.walk
map.takes: a list of tree nodes
map.gives: nothing; it fills the out list in place
map.story:
walk(ns) adds each node in ns to out, then does the same for the children of that node.
Example: ns holds one node F01 with one child F01.1; out becomes [F01, F01.1].
A parent always comes before its own children. A node with no children ends that branch. The list out belongs to nodes_of, so walk(ns) returns nothing.
map.text: walk(ns) -> None — adds every node in the list ns, and every node under it, to the out list of nodes_of

children.text:
walk = the recursive helper inside nodes_of that collects a tree of nodes into one flat list.
It takes ns, a list of nodes at one level, and writes into the out list of nodes_of instead of returning a value.

For each node t in ns: put t into out, then, when t has a children list, call walk on those children.
The parent enters out before its children, so out holds the whole tree in top-down order.

map.name: number
map.takes: the list of block roots, in file order
map.gives: an id string set on every node, in place
map.story:
number(tree) gives every node in the tree an id.
Example: the second block root gets the id F02, and its first two beats get F02.1 and F02.2.
The ids follow file order. The function changes the nodes in place and returns nothing.
map.text: number(tree) -> None — gives every node of the map an id: F01, F02 for the top-level blocks, and dotted numbers under each of them

children.text: take the tree of block roots and go through the top-level nodes in file order, counting from 1

t["id"] = the label of this top-level block, F01, F02, F03 and so on.

k = a one-item list that counts the children numbered so far.
It is a list, not a plain number, so the nested helper can change the count it holds.

hand the children of this root to walk(), which sets an id like F01.1 on each of them and on every node below them.
A root with no children gets an empty list, so nothing happens.

map.name: number.walk
map.takes: a list of child nodes
map.gives: an id string on each node, nothing returned
map.story:
walk(ns) gives every node under one root an id like F01.3.
Example: under the root F01, the first child gets id F01.1 and the second gets F01.2.
The counter k is shared, so numbers keep rising through deeper levels. A child of the second node gets F01.3. Nodes without children stop the descent.
map.text: walk(ns) -> None — sets an id on every node in ns and on every node below them, counting with the shared k

children.text:
take each node c in the list ns and raise the shared counter k by one, then

c["id"] = the root's id, a dot, and the new count

k lives outside walk(ns), so the numbers rise across the whole tree and do not restart at each level
when a node holds its own children, walk(ns) calls itself on them, so nodes at every depth get an id from the same counter

map.name: owner_of
map.takes: the map tree of root nodes and their children
map.gives: a line number to node id table
map.story:
owner_of(tree) says which text of the map owns each line of the file.
Example: a leaf node, a node with no children, with id "F01.2" and lines [[3, 5]] gives {3: "F01.2", 4: "F01.2", 5: "F01.2"}.
Only leaf nodes put lines in the result, because a parent shares its lines with its children.
A line that no leaf covers is not in the result.
map.text: owner_of(tree) -> dict from line number to node id — says which text of the map owns each line of the file

children.text:
owner = the table that maps each file line to the id of the node that holds it

It starts empty and fills as the tree is read.

Read every node of the tree with nodes_of, and keep only the nodes with no children.
For each such node, mark every line in each of its spans with that node's id.
Parent nodes are skipped because their lines already belong to their children, and the deepest node is the true owner.
Give the finished table back, so a caller can ask which node owns a line.

map.name: links
map.takes: the source file path and the line-to-node-id map
map.gives: one row per shared name, with its defining node and its using nodes
map.story:
links(path, owner) reports which text nodes share a name.
Example: cells_of is defined at line 67 and called at line 441. If owner says line 67 belongs to F02 and line 441 belongs to F12.5, links gives {"name": "cells_of", "def": "F02", "used": ["F12.5"]}.
The jedi library reads the names. Names that come from another file are dropped. A name that no other node uses gives no row. For a file that is not Python, the result is an empty list.
map.text: links(path, owner) -> list of rows — finds every name defined and used in this one file, and reports which text nodes define it and which text nodes use it

children.text:
links(path, owner) takes the file and owner, the map from a line number to the id of the text node that holds that line.

Only Python files have names to read, so any other suffix gives an empty list.

Set up the three things the search needs:

p = the absolute path of the file, used later to test that a name belongs to this file

script = the jedi view of the file, the tool that finds names and their references

rows = the list that collects the finished link rows

Step through every name jedi finds in the file, and skip a name whose definition is in another file.

An import like ast or json points out of the file, and the reader cannot open it here.

src = the id of the text node that holds the line of the definition.

When owner has no id for that line, no node can be the source of the link, so skip the name.

used = the sorted ids of the text nodes that hold the other lines where the name is read.

References on lines owner does not know are dropped, and references inside the defining node itself are dropped, because a link to itself tells the reader nothing.
Keep the name only when some other node uses it, and record the row: its name, the node that defines it, and the nodes that use it.
Give back all the rows, which the reader turns into clickable name links between the texts.

map.name: row_of
map.takes: a cell number, a cell, and the file lines
map.gives: one text line that describes the cell
map.story:
row_of(i, c, lines) makes one line that describes a cell for the prompt.
Example: cell 2 holds lines 370-370, so row_of gives "2: lines 370-370 | spans = ...".
A cell with several line ranges lists them all, separated by commas. The code shown is always the first line of the first range, with the indent removed.
map.text: row_of(i, c, lines) -> string — writes one cell as a numbered prompt line with its line ranges and its first line of code

children.text:
take the cell number i, the cell c, and all the file lines

spans = the cell's line ranges as text, like "370-370" or "12-14, 20-21"
the reader of the prompt needs these numbers to point a beat at real lines

give back one line: the cell number, then the line ranges, then the first line of code in the cell with its indent removed
the code sample lets the model see what the cell is about without reading the file again

map.name: write_node
map.takes: a map node and its indent string
map.gives: the JSON text of that node and every node under it
map.story:
write_node(t, ind) prints one node of the map as JSON text, with its children under it.
A node with children ends with a "children" list, one child per line, indented two spaces more.
Example: write_node({"id": "F01.2", "layer": 1, "text": "keep the digits", "lines": [[3, 4]]}, "  ") gives '  {"id": "F01.2", "layer": 1, "text": "keep the digits", "lines": [[3, 4]]}'.
A root node has a name, so it also prints name, layer, calls, takes, gives, and story.
The function writes text, not a data object, so the field order in the map file stays fixed.
map.text: write_node(t, ind) -> string — turns one map node and its children into indented JSON text, one field per node on a single line

children.text:
head = the JSON text of this node, opened with the indent and the id field

Every later step adds more fields to head.

Add the fields that depend on the kind of node:

a node with a name is a block root, so it gets name, layer, calls, takes and gives, plus story when it has one

a node with no name is a beat, so it gets only its layer
Add the two fields every node has: its text and its line ranges.
A node with no children is complete: close the brace and return the line.
A node with children calls write_node on each child with two more spaces of indent, then returns the node with the child lines inside a "children" list.

map.name: write_map
map.takes: an output path and the map object
map.gives: nothing; the file on disk holds the map
map.text: write_map(path, m) -> None — writes the finished map object to a JSON file that a person can read

children.text:
rows = the link records of m["links"], each as JSON on its own line

links_part = that list wrapped in brackets, or the text [] when there are no links

One link per line keeps the file readable for a person.
trows and terms_part = the same treatment for m["terms"]: one term record per line, or [] when the list is empty
tree = the JSON text of every top-level map node, from write_node with a four-space indent, joined one node after the other
join the file name, links_part, terms_part, and tree into one JSON object and write it to path as UTF-8

map.name: compile_block
map.takes: one block with its cells, the file text, the statement spans, and the callee context
map.gives: the checked tree node for that block and its terms
map.story:
compile_block builds the prompt for one block, asks claude, and returns the checked node.
Example: a 5-cell block gives a node with a text, takes, gives, story, and 3 beat children.
Each failed check goes back to claude in note, together with every rule broken before.
A block of one cell gets no children. After 8 failed tries the program stops with sys.exit.
map.text: compile_block(bl, cells, name, code, lines, stmts, ess, ctx) -> (node, terms) — builds the prompt for one block, asks claude, and retries until the answer passes every check

children.text:
compile_block takes one block bl and the cells that belong to it, and gives back the finished node for that block.

bstmts = the statements of the file that sit fully inside the block's line ranges.
The checker needs them, because it must reject a beat that holds only part of a statement.

stext = the prompt section that lists those statements as indented line ranges.
It stays empty when the block holds no statement, so a file that is not python gets no such section.

Two more fields the prompt needs:

label — the block's function name with parentheses, or the words the top-level script code when the block has no node
span — the block's line ranges written as text

rows = one prompt line per cell, each one written by row_of with the cell number, its line ranges, and its first line of code.

base = the full PROMPT with the file, the label, the span, the context ctx, the cell rows, and the cell count filled in.

Three values that carry the retry state:

note — the extra text added after the prompt when an answer was bad, empty on the first try
errs — every rule that the answers broke so far
m — the last answer, kept so the repair note can show it back
Try at most 8 times to get one answer that passes every check.

ask_claude sends base plus note and returns the answer as a dict.
check_block then tests every shape rule and gives back the root, the story, the terms, and the beats. It raises an error when the answer breaks a rule, and the except part below catches that error.

node = the block's entry in the tree: the root text, takes, gives, story, and all its lines joined by merge.

Each beat becomes one child node with its own text and its own merged lines. The children are added only when the block has more than one cell, because a block of one cell needs no step below it.

The function prints one count line and returns the node together with the cleaned terms.

When a check fails, print the error, add it to errs, and make a new note: the last answer, the rule it broke, and all the rules broken before.
The next try sends that note with the prompt, so claude repairs the answer and does not make the same mistake again.
When all 8 tries fail, stop the full program with sys.exit and name the block that failed.

map.name: main
map.takes: a source file path from the command line
map.gives: a map.json file beside that source file
map.story:
main() reads one source file and writes map.json next to it.
Example: main() on decompile.py explains every block with claude, then writes map.json in that folder.
A block is explained after the blocks it calls, so its prompt holds their meanings.
The layer number from layers_of() sets that order.
A block with no valid answer after 8 tries stops the run.
map.text: main() -> None — reads the file named on the command line and writes map.json, one explained text for every block and every beat inside it

children.text:
path = the source file named as the first command line argument.
src and lines hold its text, whole and split per line.
The assert stops the run at once when the file has no non-blank line, because an empty file has nothing to explain.

code = the whole file with a line number and a bar in front of every line.
This is the form the prompt shows to claude, so claude and the checker count lines the same way.

Two readings of the file, both from the same source text:

cells — cells_of() cuts the file into the smallest line ranges a text can explain.
stmts — statements() lists every Python statement with its depth and its line range.

ess = the essential lines, the lines a beat is judged on.
A line is essential when it belongs to a statement that holds no smaller statement inside it, and when it is not blank.
The check for a beat that cuts a statement uses ess, so blank lines and outer wrapper lines never make a beat look wrong.

The call structure of the file, in five steps:

blocks — blocks_of() splits the file into one block per function or class, plus a script block.
body — the top-level statements of the file, which calls_of() needs for the script block.
names — the set of block names, so a call is only counted when it points at a block of this file.
calls — calls_of() per block, the names each block uses.
lay — layers_of() per block, one more than the deepest block it calls.

parts = the cells of each block, keyed by block name.
Every cell goes to the one block whose line ranges hold all of the cell, so no cell is explained twice and none is lost.

Three collectors for the loop that follows:

done — the finished root node of every block already explained.
tout — the terms of the whole file, in the order they first appear.
tseen — the term words already in tout, so a repeated term is added once.

Explain the blocks from the lowest layer up, so a caller is always explained after the blocks it calls.
ctx = the one-line meaning, takes and gives of every block this block calls, taken from done.
The prompt carries ctx, so the text of a caller can speak of a callee at its level instead of repeating its inside.

compile_block() asks claude for this block and retries until the answer passes every check.
It gives back the root node with its beats as children, and the terms the story defines.
Add each new term to tout with the block that coined it, and skip a term tseen already holds.

Finish the root node of the block with the facts claude did not produce:

name — the block name.
layer — its layer number from lay.
calls — the block names it calls.
lines — its line ranges in the file.

Then store it in done, where the next callers read it as their ctx.
Put the roots back in file order, then number() gives every node an id, and owner_of() builds the table that says which node owns each line.

m = the finished map: the file name, the shared names links() found, the terms, and the tree.
write_map() writes it to map.json beside the source file.
Print the counts of the run — blocks, texts, links, terms, claude calls — and the path written.
